# The Little Peasant.

There is an old saying or common proverb <note>original Latin: proverbium</note> among us Germans: after great suffering, great joy usually follows; and so also the reverse <note>original Latin: Sic & è contra</note>. Unfortunately, it happened this way to me a few years ago—just as it has happened to others who began without a true basis or foundation—as I will relate at length. For when I believed I held the whole world in my hands, I ended up with less than nothing. This was because my glass vessel, in which I had placed all my hopes for prosperity, shattered with a great bang; the chemical materials splattered my <term>silent philosophers</term> <note>original Latin: mutos philosophos; this refers to alchemical books of emblems and symbolic images that "speak" without words</note> and books here and there, causing great damage and loss, of which I must for now remain silent. I was so paralyzed, struck dumb, and terrified by this unexpected misfortune that, in my sorrow and distress, I did not know where I was, what I was doing, or how I should proceed. For all my joy, pleasure, and delight had been transmuted and changed into sheer poison and bitter gall, rather than into the gold and silver I had hoped for.

<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<summary>The author describes a disastrous alchemical experiment in which his equipment shattered, destroying his books and plunging him into despair. This failure serves as a cautionary tale about practicing alchemy without a proper foundation.</summary>

<keywords>alchemy, failed experiment, transmutation, The Little Peasant, silent philosophers, gold, silver, laboratory accident</keywords>

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative from page 1. After the despair of his alchemical failure, the author turns to prayer and theological reflection on whether such divine secrets can be granted to sinners.</meta>

### The Little [Peasant]

Now, as I came a little to my senses, I first considered my great disadvantage and loss, and began to complain and present the same, with bended knees, hot tears <note>original: Zehern (Zähren)</note>, and heartfelt sighs, to Him who lives from eternity to eternity. (For God gives and takes it as it pleases Him, and to whom He wills), earnestly praying that He would now intimately take me up and have mercy on me, so that, if possible, He would guide, lead, and show me the right way to the mirror of His Majesty through the Spirit of Truth and Wisdom. ### The Little Treatise

<margin>x</margin> When they speak of a single thing, it is the **Salt of Metals** <note>original: *Sal metallorum*</note>, the **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: *Lapis philosophorum*</note>. <margin>x</margin> And know, if the bath is not governed in such a way that both natures rise together, but rather only one alone, then you shall never enjoy nor partake in their scent; therefore, pay close attention to this remarkable **operation** <term>Operation: A specific, controlled stage of the alchemical process or "Work"</term>.

# Baur.

I doubted that very much, all too sadly. The worst part was that the common blacksmiths and goldsmiths accused me before the City Council, claiming that I was making charcoal expensive for them. They argued they could not maintain their trade or their civic livelihood, and therefore *consequently* <note>original: *per consequentiam*</note> they could pay no interest or taxes <term>Schoß</term> <note>A medieval term for a direct tax on property or income paid to the city authorities.</note> to the Council and the common city, because I paid so dearly for the charcoal simply so that I could secure it before they did. They kept this up for so long that the Council eventually issued a prohibition against me, further indicating that I should desist *from the handling of charcoal* <note>original: *à tractatione carbonum*</note> and behave according to my own profession. *In short* <note>original: *In summa*</note>, the trouble was so great that I was forced to tear down my furnaces, move away from that place, and seek a good friend who would provide me with the necessary money so that I could wait for the <term>Universal</term> <note>The "Universal" refers to the Great Work of the Philosopher's Stone, which was a much longer and more expensive process than the "Particular" methods used for quick profit.</note> with more peace of mind. Yet, I told no one what I had in my mind. These same *tribulations* <note>original: *tribulationes*</note>, involving travel and other inconveniences, lasted nearly into the third year. God knows how it weighed on my heart that I knew and was capable of everything, yet still could not put my hand to the Work. I thought back and forth: perhaps God does not yet want to have it so, or will not permit it.

> *For wherever the fates drag us and pull us back, there we must follow.* <note>A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book V, line 709: "Quo res cumque cadunt, flectit Fortuna; sequamur. / Nam quò nos fata trahunt, retrahuntque, eò nos sequi oportet."</note>

On my journey, I *conferred* <note>original: *conferierte*</note> with learned people and became ever more knowledgeable; they *passed on* <note>original: *tradierten*</note>...

# Peasant. 25

...I will not trouble you much with the *handling* <note>original: *Tractation*</note> of coals now, for I have no need of them at present.

Now, as the poisonous vapors departed from the stone, our two flowers—of which the Peasant had spoken—appeared quite gradually. Yet I became aware of the White one sooner, for the Red was not yet graded <note>original: *gradiert*; in alchemy, "grading" refers to intensifying the color or quality of a substance to reach a higher state of perfection.</note>. By this I recognized that it was the *female* <note>original: *Weiblin*; in the symbolic language of alchemy, the "feminine" principle is associated with volatility, moisture, and the color white.</note>, because it was so fleeting and *volatile*.

### On the Little Peasant

Therefore, the white flower naturally precedes the red; indeed, the red is hidden within the white. Thus, the **red tincture** <note>The "Red Tincture" or "Red Lion" is the final stage of the Great Work, capable of transmuting metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</note> unfailingly follows the first, without any addition of foreign materials, solely through the completion of the **cooking** <note>The alchemical process of "digestion," where steady heat is applied to the matter over a long period.</note>. 

Thus our work, or **subject** <note>In alchemy, the "subject" is the raw starting material, also known as the "Prime Matter."</note>, is and remains a single thing from beginning to end; for it contains everything within itself that one desires. Therefore, the **Philosophers** <note>Alchemical writers often referred to themselves and their predecessors as "Philosophers," meaning those who seek the wisdom of nature.</note> say: **it dissolves itself** <note>original Latin: *solvit seipsum*</note>, **it coagulates itself** <note>original Latin: *coagulat seipsum*</note>. It turns itself black, white, and red; it kills and awakens itself; it cleanses and <term>fixes</term> <note>To "fix" a substance means to make a volatile or gaseous material solid and resistant to heat.</note> itself; and in short, it does everything of its own accord, if only the <term>artist</term> <note>The alchemist or practitioner performing the operation.</note> pays heed to the fire and, when one must steer, holds the rudder. 

This single thing allows itself to be grasped and handled at the beginning, but at the end, it allows itself to be seen and mastered. For it is one body and a **chaos** <note>original Latin: *Chaos*; a term for the primal, unformed state of the matter before it is organized by the alchemical process.</note> in which the highest power and the noblest **spirits** <note>original Latin: *Spiritus*; the vital, volatile essences believed to dwell within physical matter.</note> lie hidden—the greatest ever found in Nature. This power, however, sleeps within this **subject**, lying still and locked away as if in a prison or a chest; it cannot move nor help itself. 

But the artist must awaken it with the external fire, loosen its bonds, and direct it toward growth; he must give it air so that it may move, so that which is hidden may come forth, and through the proper maintenance of <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of turning a solid into vapor and back again, intended to purify the substance.</note>, it may reach its perfection. 

The first labor of this work is to make it into a **viscous substance** <note>original: *Viscosa*; a thick, sticky state of the matter during its transformation.</note>, unharmed and without loss

### Regarding the little beetles <note>original: *Bawren*. While this literally means "farmers," in early modern German it was a common folk name for various beetles, such as the dung beetle or the cockchafer.</note>

Take a beetle or little creature—whatever **insect** <note>original: *Insectū*</note> or other small animal it may be—and let it fall into spirits <note>original: *Branntwein*</note>. Once it is killed, pull it out immediately, and while it is still warm, arrange its **limbs** <note>original: *membra*</note> and shape it as you please. Then let it cool and stiffen. Glue it to a small piece of wood in the most convenient place where it can hold (this piece of wood will later serve as the **casting sprue** <term>Gußkehl: the channel or funnel through which molten metal is poured into a mold</term>). 

Next, prepare a thin paste or mash made of **spar** <term>Spaat: a mineral like feldspar or gypsum, used here as a heat-resistant mold material</term> that has been burnt three times, re-moistened with water each time, and well-beaten, with a little burnt **bole** <term>bolus: a fine, iron-rich clay used to give body to the mixture</term> mixed in; or alternatively, a paste of **plaster** <note>original: *Gips*</note> and lukewarm water. Dip the fly or the little creature into it and pull it out immediately, so that some of the thin mash adheres and forms a skin. Let it dry, then dip it again; continue this until it becomes firm enough to withstand another outer coating.

Then one burns out the fly inside and lets the mold glow red-hot. And so that everything comes out and the **mold** <note>original: *matrix*</note> is cleaned out perfectly, let a little **mercury** <note>original: *Quecksilber*</note> run through it, which seeks out whatever might still be stuck inside. 

Then pour into it an alloy of tin, containing a little lead and even less **bismuth** <note>original: *Wißmat*</note>. 

But if you wish to cast gold or silver into it, then—when the gold or silver is fluid and moving—throw a little **sublimate** <term>mercury sublimate: a chemical used here as a flux to help the metal flow into the finest details of the mold</term> into the **crucible** <note>original: *Tigel*</note> onto the gold. Before it has completely evaporated, pour it out; thus you have formed your little creature, so subtle...

# About the Little Peasant <note>original: *vber den kleinen Bawren*; this likely refers to a specific type of beetle or common insect used in casting, or perhaps a title for this section of observations on nature.</note>

We desire to sink a soul and a life into the prepared *body* <note>original: *Corpori*</note>; but that is the work of God alone. The rest is nothing but a shadow and a representation <note>original: *Mahlwerck*; literally "painted work" or "image," implying that art can only imitate the appearance of life</note>. We now handle the question among us: from where does life come to such little animals—the *insects*—and how is it poured into them? Namely, it comes from the life-giving spirit, which is indeed scattered <note>original: *spargiert*</note> everywhere in the air and slips into the nearest prepared *body*, but in our box <note>likely referring to the casting mold or a controlled experimental environment</note> it is condensed. The entire world, however, is full of this *vital spirit* <note>original: *Spiritus vitalis*</note>.

A *philosopher* said in times past—just as the *Brahmins* <note>original: *Brachmanni*; refers to the priestly caste of India, often cited in Renaissance texts as ancient keepers of wisdom</note>, the Indian *philosophers*, let it be heard: The world is an animal. He did not speak out of ignorance. You see how this animal breathes, what a strong breath it lets in and out everywhere; you see how all the limbs of this animal stir; there is nothing but spirit and life in it. Observe, moreover, what *reason* <note>original: *ration*</note>, craftsmanship, order, and wonderful, inscrutable character, nature, and property it has in its works and in all its deeds.

And this work of God is greater and more wonderful than you might think; therefore, the man did not speak poorly in saying that the entire world is an animal. It can withstand the *definition* of an animal (and still have something left over), for this animal has life, movement within itself, and all other *requirements* <note>original: *requisita*</note> and *properties* <note>original: *propria*</note> of an animal with and within itself.

For example <note>original: *exempli gratia*</note>, poison lies hidden in many herbs, stones, animals, **mercurial substances** <note>original: *Mercuriis*; here referring to various volatile or metallic preparations</note>, and other **bodies** <note>original: *corporibus*</note>; in one it is more present and stronger than in another. ### Commentaries

You certainly must not look for the right faith among them first; for they are commonly perverse, confused, at odds among themselves, and help to suppress and persecute the truth along with its adherents.

With the words above, however, the author does not only intend the **philosopher** <term>Philosopher; *Philosophum*, here referring to an alchemist or seeker of wisdom</term> to be understood by the "peasant"—he who instructs him in **physics** <term>Physics; *physicis*, the study of the laws of nature</term> (though he is the peasant himself)—but also intends, through this peasant's clothing, to reveal the nature and property of the **matter**. He shows how the work behaves during the **cooking** <note>A term for alchemical digestion or the application of heat to a substance</note> and the preparation of the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Philosopher's Stone; *philosophischen Steins*</term>, and how it is produced gradually over time.

Namely, in the beginning there is the **subject** <term>Subject; *Subjectum*, the base material or "prima materia"</term> which one receives from Nature's hand. Within it, the **universal tincture** <term>Universal Tincture; *Universal Tinctur*, the transformative essence</term> of all metals, animals, and plants lies hidden, like a raw, unrefined **body** <term>Body; *Corpus*</term>. It has a gray mantle or coat wrapped around it, just as peasants in the field during winter commonly have little decoration about them, but are instead hung and surrounded everywhere on their beards and bodies with **hoarfrost** <note>original: *Dufft*, here meaning frost or vapor</note> and icicles.

Nevertheless, many of them have great understanding in their heads, though one cannot see this with the eyes. One must not judge or evaluate the internal virtue and skill by the outward appearance; just as, conversely, many a dreamer and coarse, ignorant person hides beneath a velvet cap and long cloak or silken garment.

It usually falls off or out by itself, if one only holds a hat underneath so as not to lose it.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the alchemist’s role, emphasizing that the "Magisterium" is a natural process where the human "Artist" acts only as a facilitator or guide to Nature’s innate, God-given powers.</meta>

<page-num>72</page-num>
<header>Commentaries</header>
<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<margin>+</margin>
If any natural thing exists in the world, then the completion and the <term>Magisterium; *magisterium*, the mastery or perfected process of the Great Work</term> of our <term>philosophical Stone; *philosophischen Steins*, the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and healing</term> is natural. It is not the work of a man, but entirely the work of Nature. The <term>Artist; here referring to the alchemist</term> contributes nothing to it, except that he directs Nature toward growth (just as any farmer or vine-dresser does with his fruits and plantings), clears all obstacles from the path as previously mentioned, and is so sharp-witted in understanding and possesses such great grace from God that he governs its course and, when necessary, applies a bit <note>original: *Gebiß*; a metaphor for "bridling" or controlling the intensity of the chemical reaction</note>.

For God, at the very beginning of Creation, implanted such power in this creature <note>original: *Creatur*; in this context, it refers to the primary matter or the Stone as a created thing</note> above all other creatures, and He still endows it daily. If this were not so, it would be impossible for any person on Earth to bring such a work to its desired end or to produce any use from it. 

Furthermore, since He endowed man with reason above all other animals, so that he might recognize His works and not leave them uninvestigated: this man—and those whom He has awakened for this purpose—has a duty to rightly take up this high and deeply hidden work and great secret. He must seek out this treasure, open the chest, and, for the glory and honor of his Creator, bring forth the most precious pearl <note>original: *Berlen*; likely a metaphor for the purified essence of the Stone</note> and the noblest essence that Nature has ever held within her as long as the world has stood. He should enjoy it, apply it to the welfare of needy people, and offer Him eternal praise and thanks.

->### concerning the Little Peasant<-

agents: For no thing can bring itself forth; *for like does not act upon its like* <note>original: *simile namque non agit in sibi simile*</note>. In the *generation of things* <note>original: *in generationibus rerum*</note> there must be a movement and an impulse. If a movement is to occur, it must come from *opposites* <note>original: *Contrariis*</note>; and first there must be one thing that moves, and then another that is moved. Therefore, in all these works, there is *action and passion* <note>original: *Actio & passio*; referring to the active and passive principles of "acting" and "being acted upon"</note>. 

This, I say, is the general order of God in the birth of all creatures. When an active principle <note>original: *Wirckents*</note> finds itself within the *object* <note>original: *Objecto*</note> or the passive subject, and follows its orderly course, it gives birth at the end of the work to a third thing, bringing a new form and *essence* <note>original: *Essents*</note>. Then the active is entirely separated from the passive (or from the new form that has been introduced), and a completed work stands upon the site.

Thus the author says here in our work that there are two pieces: one of the male, the other of the female gender, etc. This is nothing other than <term>Sulphur: In alchemical theory, the active, solar, and "combustible" principle associated with the soul and heat</term> and <term>Mercury: The passive, lunar, and "volatile" principle associated with the spirit and moisture</term>. For from these two pieces the <term>Philosophers' Stone: Latin: *Lapis philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting physical and spiritual perfection</term> must and shall be made. 

<term>Mercury</term> is of a moist and cold nature. <term>Sulphur</term> is the inward, innate heat, or the fire that sticks within the <term>Mercury</term>; it is hot and dry. So now, the heat and dryness of the <term>Sulphur</term> must gradually overcome the moisture and coldness of the <term>Mercury</term> during the <term>decoction: The process of maturing or "cooking" a substance through steady heat to achieve a state of perfection</term>, until in time the <term>Sulphur</term> exalts the <term>Mercury</term> and makes it equal to itself. That is the <term>sublimation: In alchemy, the purification of a substance by vaporizing it and allowing it to solidify again, symbolizing the elevation of the material to a higher state</term> of the philosophers.

In this way, a moderate fire is produced from both of them at once. Then there is the weight, the *Proportion* and the balancing of nature; and immediately, through the understanding and will of the *Master* <note>The "Master" refers to the practicing alchemist directing the work.</note>, everything can become one.

The matter is desirous of the form, and the form of the matter, like a wife for her husband, until at last these two are entirely reconciled and become thoroughly one.

### Commentaries

<margin>+</margin>
Like and like gladly join together. For the **tincture** <note>original: *Tinctur*; the concentrated essence or medicine capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</note> that is to enter into the metals, pushing aside their crude **sulfur** and permanently coloring the metal's **mercury**, must be entirely pure and of the highest subtlety. Such subtlety, however, is attained when the noble **spirits** and **homogeneous parts** <term>partes homogeneas: parts that are of the same kind or nature</term> are driven together with gentle warmth, and are released and separated from the coarse, earthy parts, and then returned to the purified bodies. **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a legendary figure in alchemy whose writings were considered authoritative.</note> says: *Spirits not cleansed of the dregs of the earth do not enter metallic bodies; and therefore they do not transform them, because that which does not enter, does not transform.* <note>original Latin: *Spiritus à fæculentia terræ non mundati, non ingrediuntur corpora metallica: Ideóque nec alterant siquidem non alterat, quod non ingreditur.*</note> Again, **Geber** says: *He who knows how to mix and unite spirits and bodies during the preparation knows one of the greatest secrets in this art.* <note>original Latin: *Qui in præparatione noverit commiscere & amicari spiritus & corpora: scit unum de secretis in hac arte maximum.*</note>

And Nature herself does all this, provided only that the **Artist** <note>original: *Artist*; the alchemist or practitioner of the Hermetic Art.</note> does not disturb her, but instead allows the proper solar heat to be applied and permits no other **accidents** <note>original: *accidens*; unexpected external interferences or impurities that might ruin the chemical reaction.</note> to occur. Therefore, the **laborant** <note>The worker or laboratory assistant.</note> needs no further art, curiosity, or other subtleties to be used here. Let him only see to it that he provides for the process from the outside, and let him be satisfied with that. For Nature can help herself along and work sufficiently toward perfection. She has the movement within herself, has her certain intent, and follows a single path—and she does so in a more certain and better order than can be devised by any man or prescribed to her in the **creation** of any generated thing.

# Concerning the Little Peasant <note>original: *vber den kleinen Bawren*; this refers to the title of the work, *Der kleine Bauer* (The Little Peasant), a famous alchemical treatise attributed to Johann Grasshoff.</note>
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

You see indeed that Nature everywhere—as also in the birth of metals—uses no special subtleties or extraneous labors. She does not exert herself with common distilling, subliming, cohobating, or calcining <term>calcining: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or cause oxidation</term>, as the common crowd is fond of such manual tricks, and she avoids the ways that lead to the destruction of Nature: For in the mountains, one finds neither distillers nor laboratory workers. 

<margin>+</margin> Instead, Nature does everything of herself and carries out her work in a completely simple and modest way.

Therefore, whoever wishes to create fruit and bring his work to an end, let him leave Nature undisturbed, and instead take care only for the foment <term>foment: a source of steady warmth or incubation, similar to a medicinal fomentation or a brooding hen's heat</term>. This may be seen with wonder in a walnut, a chestnut, a pomegranate—indeed, in all other fruits and plants, as well as in the birth of all animals. See how, out of an initially mixed, unformed, tasteless, wild Chaos <note>original: *Chao*; referring to the "Prima Materia" or the disorganized state of matter before it is perfected</note>, through the slow cooking of Nature, such a beautiful, well-tasting, and most artfully formed fruit is finally brought forth. 

Such a clever, artful, and wonderful separation is achieved: the husks, the casing, the shells, the skin, the burr <note>original: *Igel*; literally "hedgehog," referring here to the prickly outer shell of a chestnut</note>, the bark, and the chaff set themselves aside in one place, while the inner, well-tasting, and ripened kernel—along with its seed and hidden internal power to propagate its own kind and continue its race—gathers in another place. And the outer part preserves the inner during the decoction <term>decoction: the process of heating a substance to extract its essence or ripen it through internal "cooking"</term>, helping it toward maturation.

When hailstones <note>original: *Stein*; literally "stones"</note> are formed up there because of intense cold, which then fall down in heaps or are driven by the wind—notwithstanding their great weight—this is a hard **concretion** <note>original: *Concretio*; a solidification of matter</note> where the water coagulates and becomes **little stones** <note>original: *Lapilli*; hailstones</note> that are crystalline.

Mist, dew, and frost are all caused according to how moisture, heat, and cold are found in this "glass" and **sublimation vessel** <note>original: *sublimatorio*; an alchemical vessel used to heat a substance until it becomes vapor and then collects as a solid</note>, and how the earth exhales <note>original: *erhaliert*</note> or how the air above is composed.

When it thunders, lightens, strikes, and cracks, it happens because the "work" is overdriven, the **place** <note>original: *locus*</note> is too narrow, and too much heat is given. Strong trapped heat and surrounding cold fight one another, and the process proceeds with violence and is overdriven; for **opposing qualities** <note>original: *contrariæ qualitates*; such as hot versus cold or dry versus moist</note> are found there which cannot tolerate each other. Therefore, it must either have air, or the glass must bang and burst, or it cracks.

<margin>+</margin>
These are purely natural things, the likes of which also occur in **Alchemy** and its labors, for they have the same way of working. Thus, Alchemy does nothing outside of **Physics** <note>original: *Physic*; in the 17th century, this referred to the general study of the natural world</note>, and Physics performs nothing but chemical processes. > And that which the **elemental and celestial virtues** <note>original: *virtutes elementales & cœlestes*; the powers of the four elements and the influence of the stars</note> do there in natural vessels: This same [thing]...

# Commentary

...[as] they do in artificial vessels. Provided, however, that the artificial ones are well-fashioned after the manner of natural ones.

When one moves from the upper to the lower—from the air down here to the circumference of the earth—it is there that the **physical and chemical operations** <note>original: *physica & chemica operationes*</note> of Nature truly begin.

For in the changing and breaking open of all things, what does Nature drive other than pure **chemical works** <note>original: *operas chemicas*</note>? And what does the chemist drive other than **physical works** <note>original: *operas Physicas*</note>? Is it not purely **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrificieren*; the breaking down of matter through decay</note>, **digestion** <note>original: *digerieren*; the application of steady heat to mature a substance</note>, **purification** <note>original: *mundificieren*</note>, **separation** <note>original: *separieren*</note>, and **gathering** <note>original: *congregiren*</note>? Nothing else. An eternal **arising and passing away** <note>original: *Ortus & Interitus*; the cycle of birth and death or creation and destruction</note> of all things—one thing goes under, the other comes forth. The world and all its created things turn upon these two hinges, and all of this happens through the steps mentioned above. Why is it necessary to give examples? Think on the matters yourself. In the procreation of **plants** <note>original: *vegetabilium*</note> as well as **animals** <note>original: *Animalium*</note>, does Nature not maintain the four **powers** <note>original: *Potentias*</note> or **virtues** <note>original: *Virtutem*</note>: the **Attractive**, **Digestive**, **Retentive**, and **Expulsive**? This drives the work, and she proceeds in such an order even beneath the ground in the **generation of metals and minerals** <note>original: *generatione Metallorum & Mineralium*</note>.

<margin>x x</margin>
Precisely this, and nothing else, is also what a true **chemist** <note>original: *Chemicus*</note> pursues; and through such steps Nature also runs in the finishing and building up, or the **generation of our Stone** <note>original: *generando nostro lapide*; the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Nature **dissolves** <note>original: *solviert*</note> and **congeals** <note>original: *congeliert*</note>; the chemist does so as well. The chemist **moistens** <note>original: *imbibiert*</note> and **dries** <note>original: *exsicciert*</note>; Nature does so as well.

They both separate the subtle from the coarse, and...

# Concerning the Little Peasant.

...[his outward] appearance is rough, unrefined, and worthless. But inwardly, in his hidden part, when one strips off his **smock** <note>original: *Küttel*; a simple, coarse tunic worn by laborers.</note>, he possesses a great and wonderful power. This power is naturally implanted in him through a specific **constellation of the heavens** <note>original: *Constellation*; in alchemy and astrology, the specific alignment of stars at the moment of creation or birth that determines inner properties.</note>, such that his equal is not to be found on earth. For the birth-hour of this **peasant** <note>original: *Bawren*; here referring both to the literal farmer and the metaphorical base matter in the alchemical process.</note> may just as easily have fallen **under a lucky star of heaven** <note>original: *sub felici sydere coeli*</note> as that of a great doctor, prince, king, or any other person. One learns indeed that with God there is no **partiality** <note>original: *Respect*; meaning God does not favor people based on their social status.</note>, for He is wonderful in the way He adorns His creatures with gifts.

And this special, bestowed power, implanted by God and nature in this peasant, has been certainly recognized and learned by this Inquirer and **Philosopher** <note>original: *Philosophus*; likely referring to the alchemist seeking hidden truths.</note>. Otherwise, he would not have believed that peasants were also people, and would not have come to this place of wonder. For men always look only upon that which appears outwardly, which has a luster and an impressive appearance; they hold in honor whatever is expensively clothed, and always wish to deal with gold, silver, and similar costly things.

But how the author noticed under which planets the peasants are **aligned** <note>original: *constelliert*</note>, and by what **reasons** <note>original: *rationibus*</note> he came upon the path and to the understanding that allowed him to afterwards recognize the noble peasants: this I can well perceive. It was inscribed in him by the **finger of God**. And whoever wishes to know this and arrive at it must be enlightened by God.

### Commentaria

<margin>+</margin>Nature itself teaches you and leads us by the hand toward the truth and to the very foundation. It likewise gives you things to consider and ponder, as it would not be fitting for me to speak further here. I will only say this much: that the **peasants** <note>original: *Bawren*; here the author uses the literal farmer as a metaphor for the humble, "base" starting material in alchemy.</note> are also people. If one is ignorant or unskilled, another is all the more clever. Know, however, that wherever **leaden veins** <note>original: *Bleyische Adern*</note> and surface indicators appear on a mountain, it is rarely the case that a strong **lead vein** <note>original: *Bleygang*</note> does not lie beneath, should one sink a shaft. If you detect **glass-ore** <note>original: *Glaßerz*; a historical term for argentite or silver glance, a rich silver ore with a dark, glassy appearance.</note>, then **silver** and **copper** are present there, and so on; for commonly, the rich veins push upward toward the daylight. Who else would have discovered the **mines**? And if the **markers** <note>original: *Gemerck*; surface signs or geological clues</note> were not there, the little peasant would never have come to this place, much less lowered himself down into a **shaft**, spent his resources, and sought for **ore** in the depths without any preceding signs.

Which would have been impossible for the good man to carry out. Many a man searches for a long time and tries all sorts of **materials** <note>original: *materialia*</note>; he wishes to build and work, yet he not only lacks a vein (which alone carries the ore—outside of which there is nothing to be found in the rest of the mountain), but he is also not in the least knowledgeable about the mountain. He knows neither the way out nor in, neither the upper nor the lower, nor anything of the **hanging wall** or the **footwall** <note>original: *hangends noch ligends*; technical mining terms referring to the rock layers positioned above and below a mineral vein.</note>. He understands absolutely nothing about the **rock formation** <note>original: *Gebürg*</note>, which is why he daily pays his **tuition** <note>original: *Lehrgelt*; literally "apprentice's fee," a metaphor for the high cost of learning through failure and trial-and-error.</note>

For through such <term>imbibitions</term> <note>original: *Imbibitiones*; the process of a solid 'drinking' or absorbing a liquid</note> and the manifold addition of fresh water, one brings in many rays, much power, many sharp arrows, many <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *Spiritus*; volatile or airy essences</note>, and <term>tinting essences</term> <note>original: *tingierende Geister*; substances capable of projecting their color or nature onto others</note>, and <term>fixes</term> <note>original: *figiert*; making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand fire</note> one to the other. > The gods sell their goods for labor. <note>original Latin: *Dij bona sua vendunt laboribus*; a classical proverb meaning that divine results require hard work</note>

> It dissolves itself: it coagulates itself. <note>original Latin: *Solvit seipsum: coagulat seipsum*; a core alchemical principle where the matter acts upon itself without external additives</note>

# Concerning the Little Peasant

Folio 7. If he wishes to grasp the entire work briefly and pay close attention, etc.

First, concerning the <term>subject matter</term> <note>original Latin: "subjectum." In alchemy, this refers to the "prime matter" or the specific substance chosen to begin the transformation into the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, Nature—in the birth of metals within the crevices and veins of the mountains—and the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original Latin: "Philosophi." This refers to the "Sages" or alchemical masters of the past.</note>—who prepare their Stone outside the mountains—possess one and the same material. This material proves itself equal in strength and power, and its actions belong as much to the <term>Philosopher</term> as to Nature. For when identical <term>materials</term> <note>original Latin: "Materialia."</note>, the same furnace, the same fire, the same <term>sublimation</term> <note>A process where a substance is heated until it turns into vapor and then collected as it cools, used to purify and "exalt" the matter.</note>, operation, and effect are present, then necessarily the same work must come of it. For the artist follows Nature and maintains her process, except that he knows how to improve it in every part, to <term>correct</term> <note>original: "corrigieren."</note> and ennoble Nature. In this case, he is above Nature and a master of Nature, for he carries out his work from Nature’s foundation much higher than Nature herself, who cannot help herself in many respects: The power is indeed within her, but she often cannot bring it to completion because she lacks <term>reason</term> <note>original: "Ration." This implies that while Nature has the raw power, it lacks the conscious, directed intelligence that the human alchemist provides to reach the final goal.</note>: for you have never heard that Nature ever gave birth to the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original Latin: "Lapidem philosophorum."</note> or the <term>form of gold</term> <note>original Latin: "formam auri."</note>. Therefore, so that all things are well executed, the will of man must mingle with Nature; and where one might seek to destroy the other, he must step in and still the strife, so that peace and unity are maintained.

<meta>catchword: Further</meta>

<summary>This page explains that the alchemist (the "Artist") uses the same raw materials as Nature but uses human reason to refine and complete the work that Nature alone cannot finish, such as the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>
<keywords>subject matter, Philosopher's Stone, nature vs art, sublimation, form of gold, alchemy, the Little Peasant</keywords>

# Concerning the Little Peasant #

...were of male and female, and of different natures, which the artist and son of doctrine <note>original: "doctrinæ filius," a traditional alchemical term for an initiate or student of the hermetic arts.</note> had until now not known, or perhaps had not even noticed. Therefore, it is important to know that this, our intended Work, may be carried out in two ways; for the philosophers have undertaken different types of work.

Some have dealt with gold and silver and have thereby furthered and strengthened their Work, and thus—provided it was through the proper root—they have reached a good end. This is not to be scolded, but rather praised. And I find that many of the philosophers—indeed, the majority—proceed in this way, for this is the best and also the shortest path. Although Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), a revolutionary Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>, as well as others without doubt, has again shortened and improved this path; not indeed for the sake of the material, but in the manipulation and preparation <note>original: "præparation," the chemical processing or purification of substances.</note>, concerning the length of the cooking.

Others—among whom are a smaller portion of the moderns <note>original: "neotericis," referring to recent or contemporary authors of the seventeenth century.</note> and even the ancients—have wanted to know nothing at all of natural gold and silver, which is mined by ore-laborers in tunnels and shafts, smelted, brought under the hammer by goldsmiths, and which stirs the "bad blood" <note>A reference to the greed and moral corruption often associated with physical wealth.</note> of misers. Instead, they have carried out their Work with a single <term>subject</term> <note>original: "Subjecto." In alchemy, the "subject" is the raw, base material from which the Philosopher's Stone is extracted.</note>, just as our present, highly learned Peasant does; and that is much more elegant and more skillful.

For who could ever give everyone enough gold? If that were the case, the Art would have to be only for the princes, kings, and the wealthy of this world. In such a way, no peasant or other poor fellow could ever attain it...

...only consider any egg; here I ask you: where are the **active agent** <note>original Latin: *agens*</note> and the **passive subject** <note>original Latin: *patiens*</note> to be found in this single thing, in order to hatch a bird? ### Concerning the Little Peasant ###

...it is then no longer *common gold* <note>original: *aurum vulgi*</note>, but is now called *physical gold* <note>original: *aurum physicum*</note> and *gold of the philosophers* <note>original: *philosophorum*</note>, and *our gold* <note>original: *aurum nostrum*</note>: *for common metals become physical through preparation* <note>original: *nam vulgaria metalla præparatione fieri physica*</note>. Indeed, it happens the same way among the theologians, with the beautiful, simple, healing, and pure verses of Divine Scripture.

...[interpretations] and the explanation of philosophical sayings, according to the nature of both the intended matters and their subject.

Since this is the case—that one always finds a hundred deceivers and ignoramuses before encountering one who is truthful and knowledgeable—who would then want to bind an honest man to the testimony and faith of this or that prince or his preacher? For such a person may nevertheless err and hold a false opinion. Even if he will not admit it; for he who errs does not know or believe that he is erring.

That would be handled no differently than if one wanted to force a <term>student of chemistry</term> <note>original: *Studiosum Chemicæ*</note> to swear upon the foundation and assertions established by another ignorant <term>alchemist</term>, to accept it as a known fact, to build and set his work upon it, and—in such a difficult and hidden matter—to not use his own judgment, nor <term>raise any doubt</term> <note>original: *dubium movieren*</note>, nor rely upon his own understanding and knowledge. This is especially true since he himself may still look into the book, draw water from the true well, and learn the truth from the <term>proven philosophers</term> <note>original: *probatis Philosophis*; referring to authoritative alchemical authors like Geber or Lully</note>. But more on this elsewhere.

> <term>Artephius</term> <note>A legendary alchemist, often claimed to have lived for a thousand years through the use of the Elixir</note>: **Our water also has the power of making gold in itself, and through itself, and does not need the help of its companion: and so forth.** <note>original: *Aqua nostra habet quoque vim aurificandi in se, & per se, nec eget auxilio sui socij: & quæ sequuntur.*</note>

What is it **that all the philosophers repeatedly emphasize with this phrase: It dissolves itself, it coag[ulates]...** <note>original: *quòd omnes subinde ingeminant hanc vocem philosophi: Solvit seipsum, coag...*</note>

# About the Little Peasant

right at the start of the Work, such costs that it is impossible for the poor man to bear. <note>original: "zu erschwinden." Likely meaning to manage or survive the financial burden.</note> These are fools and ignorant people; they should study better and stay in school longer. To these one says: "He who is ignorant of the natural principles within himself (by his own reason) is already far removed from the perfection of the art." <note>original: "Qui principia naturalia in seipso (ex ratione sua) ignoraverit, is jam multum remotus est ab artis perfectione."</note> But he who knows the **first mover** <term>Primum mobile: literally "the first moved," referring here to the fundamental, active force of nature that initiates all growth and change.</term>—that is, the middle nature—and has recognized its power: he does not need the **reduction** <term>Reduction: the process of breaking down a physical metal into its "prime matter."</term> of metals, for within it lies the **white and the red** <note>These colors refer to the two stages of the Philosopher's Stone: the white tincture, which transforms metals into silver, and the red tincture, which transforms them into gold.</note> and life itself. It is a strange business. **Sophists** <term>Sophists: in alchemical literature, this term refers to deceptive or misguided practitioners who use trickery or chemical "recipes" without understanding the underlying natural philosophy.</term> warn against sophists. And that is not bad, provided they do not lead others astray at the same time with their other false **theses**, which are even worse. And yet that is also not bad. For it makes for a cautious reader and keeps the unworthy away. ## Folio 8. Further you should also be discerning, etc.

All creatures on earth are divided into three kingdoms, three sexes, or categories of created bodies, which are distinguished from one another: namely, that they are either *Vegetable*, *Animal*, or *Mineral*.

The <term>Material of the Stone</term> <note>The "Prima Materia" or starting substance required to begin the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> must not be sought among the *Vegetables* or growing things, which include all wood, all trees, shrubs, all herbs, foliage, and grass or other growths. One also must not seek it among the *Animal* creatures, such as all kinds of beasts, humans, livestock, birds, fish, nor worms, or whatever originates from these: all is unsuitable. For in the birth, increase, and <term>propagation</term> <note>original: *Fortpflanzung*; the natural process of reproduction or spreading.</note> of all things, each must remain in its own [kind]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Folio 8 regarding the three kingdoms of nature (Vegetable, Animal, and Mineral). It establishes the principle of "like produces like," arguing that the Philosopher's Stone must be derived from the mineral kingdom if it is to transform metals.</meta>

leave them be as they are, and not mix the three types and kinds of these earthly things with one another, but rather maintain that same natural distinction and let every creature follow its own path and remain in its own kingdom, according to the order of God. For no cow can become a metal: just as trees do not spring or propagate from animals and their seed, nor do humans or other animals come from the seed of metals, but rather every birth takes its seed and origin from and out of its own kind.

Now, however, from where shall we take the <term>Material</term> <note>original Latin: *Materiam*</note> and the beginning of our Stone? Answer: From the kingdom of metals and minerals. For <margin>+</margin> we certainly desire to improve and transform metals with our <term>Stone</term> <note>original Latin: *Lapide*</note>, and indeed to create them by means of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original Latin: *Mercurij*</note>.

### On the Little Peasant

# Commentaries

Tinctures are pure forms; in metals, however, there is less <term>sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur*; along with Mercury and Salt, this was one of the three primary principles of matter, representing the active, combustible "soul" of a substance.</note></term>—specifically, only as much as that particular metal requires for its own perfection. There is, however, little profit in it when one wants to make copper or lead out of gold. But we are not here now for the sake of profit, but for the sake of the Art. He who possesses the Art can also create profit; but the Art is more excellent than money, gold, or silver—know this! Therefore, because of the wonders of Nature <margin>x</margin>and Art, I do not doubt that some of the <term>philosophers <note>original: *Philosophis*; historical alchemists referred to themselves as natural philosophers.</note></term>, for the sake of pleasure and for the sake of trial, experience, and knowledge, have prepared such a thing.

For it is just as great—indeed, a much greater—<margin>x</margin>Art in Nature to make copper out of gold as it is to make gold out of copper. One is accustomed to direct things wherever one wishes through <term>fermentation <note>original: *fermentation*; in this context, a process used to "fix" or specify the outcome of a transformation, much like yeast determines the outcome of dough.</note></term>.

### Concerning the Little Peasant

Fire is dry and warm: Thus, the mentioned elements are, on one hand, contrary to one another in their **qualities** <note>original: *qualiteten*</note> and innate properties, and set **diametrically** <note>original Latin: *ex diametro*</note> against each other. On the other hand, however, they **interact** <note>original: *communicieren*</note> and each agrees with the other and possesses something in common. Thus, they hang together in an interlocking fashion, as if on a chain.

So one must not proceed here with impetuousness, but rather act reasonably and **proceed** <note>original: *procediren*</note> in an orderly way. One must bring the contrary **elements** <note>original: *elementa*</note> together on that side where they are similar to one another in **quality** <note>original: *qualitet*</note> and can tolerate each other, so that the others might also follow afterward. In this way, each is transposed into the other in an interlocking manner until all four are thoroughly changed, transformed one into the other, and finally become equal and one in all things, to prepare the **philosophers' stone** <note>original Latin: *lapidem philosophorum*, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>. 

So this is the trick: Earth and Fire agree with each other in dryness; Water and Air agree with each other in moisture. Because of these **qualities**, there would be no difficulty, and they would soon become one with each other, for they have a ladder and a handle between them. But for Fire and Water, or Earth and Air, to be converted into one another—that is difficult. It would be impossible if such a thing did not happen **with the highest reason** <note>original Latin: *cum summa ratione*</note>, and if Fire were not first transformed into Air, and Earth into Water. Through the medium of the agreeing **qualities**, the **extremes** <note>original Latin: *extrema*</note> are led to one another, each converted into the other, and finally thus reconciled...

### On the Little Peasant.

...breaking [the corrupting sulfur], so that they remain white, with the whiteness of **quicksilver** <term>original: *argenti vivi*; mercury in its liquid, "living" state</term>, after the wiping away of its first color. Likewise: the ultimate disposition and intention of nature and art is nothing other than the **stripping** <note>original: *expoliatio*; the removal of outer impurities to reveal the pure substance within.</note> of quicksilver through complete **digestion** <term>A process of slow, constant heat used to mature or purify a substance.</term> entirely away from the **corrupting sulfur**, which has cooked it, and in that same instant.

...can [hardly] express, let alone fathom. To transmute the lesser metals into the better by means of the **Stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapidem*</note>, and that within the time of a quarter-hour, is indeed a great wonder: yet it is the **philosophers'** <note>original Latin: *Philosophi*</note> least art and the first school-lesson <note>original: *Schulrecht*, referring to the basic curriculum or fundamental principles taught to a student.</note>; believe me. There are indeed higher things that are not for everyone to say, toward which men favored by God and highly gifted—men of God—later aspire and receive **angelic minds** <note>original: *Englische Gemüther*. ### Commentaries

...the correct **composition** of the materials—namely of **Sulfur** and **Mercury**, and their underlying species—which, as has been said many times now, must occur in a proper weight. Whether this weight should be taken and set as equal or unequal depends on how one chooses to understand it. It is "equal" when one takes it as it ought to be, as nature and the necessity of the Work require: 

<margin>+</margin>(Which necessity, however, is to be observed and perceived by the middle or upper tongue [of the scale] and by the **right angles**) <note>original: *angulis rectis*; refers to the precision required in balancing the alchemical scales.</note>. It is "unequal" if one wishes to look at the **ana** <term>ana|A medical and alchemical term meaning "of each an equal amount."</term>: that is, as the author here indicates, one must not take as much of the **red** as of the **white**, nor as much of the **fire** as of the **water**. This is in consideration of the fact that the **Red** is stronger and more fiery than the **White**, just as fire is more intense and hotter than water. For the **Sulfur**, as the male, is almost **choleric** <term>choleric|In the theory of the four humors, the choleric temperament is associated with yellow bile, heat, and fire.</term>: Therefore, even if he is not as heavy in weight as the **Mercury**, a small quantity of this "Spanish pepper" <note>An analogy for the spicy, heat-giving property of Sulfur.</note> is sufficient in strength and power to season a considerable weight of the female, the **Mercury**, no matter how heavy of body she is.

Dardanus says: *Know most surely that if a little gold is placed in the composition, a powerful white tincture will emerge.* <note>original: "Sciatis firmissimè, quòd si parum auri in compositione ponatur, exibit Tinctura potens candida."</note> And Plato: *Therefore, in the beginning of the work, you should unite the **Sun** by means of the **Moon**: and coagulate by means of the Sun, for from this the effects will appear, because the lower part is suppressed, since by nature the higher things rule over the lower.* <note>original: "Ideo in principio operis tu aduna Solem per Lunam: & coagula per Solem..." In alchemy, the Sun and Moon represent Gold/Sulfur and Silver/Mercury.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "little peasant" (Sulfur), emphasizing that alchemical potency is not determined by bulk volume or weight, but by concentrated internal power. # Concerning the Little Peasant #

<margin>+</margin>
It is written of Alexander the Great <note>original: *Alexandro Magno*</note>, that during his travels <note>original: *Peregrination*</note> he encountered the mighty King Darius and desired to be named a lord of that empire as well. The approaching Darius sent a warning to Alexander: that he would achieve nothing with his few men against such a mighty and great host of innumerable people as Darius had under him. Along with this message, he sent a sack full of poppy seeds <note>original: *Magsaat*</note>, stating that when Alexander could count these tiny grains, then he might also count the number of Darius’s people.

<margin>+</margin>
But Alexander sent him in return a single peppercorn <note>original: *Pfefferkorn*</note> and had this said to him: "This single grain has more heat and sharpness within it than a whole sack full of your poppy seeds."

<margin>+</margin>
Darius also became well aware of this. For Alexander defeated him with thirty thousand men and overthrew all his power—he who had believed there was no end to his people. Therefore, success does not depend on the multitude or the great crowd, but on the power and virtue <term>virtue|In alchemy, "virtue" refers to the inherent medicinal or transformative potency of a substance</term> which is gathered into small bodies <note>original: *Corporibus*</note> and driven into a narrow space; for this reason, these are all the stronger and more intense. In contrast, power that is scattered in large masses is thus rendered all the weaker.

<margin>+</margin>
Therefore, with a little saffron <note>original: *Saffran*</note> you can color a whole vessel full of water; with a little poison you can infect a large goblet <note>original: *Pocal*</note>; and with a small quantity of leaven <note>original: *Sawrteygs*; often used as a metaphor for the Alchemical Ferment</note>, you can "infect" <note>The author uses "infect" here in the sense of a transformative catalyst spreading through a medium.</note> a great mass of Mercury <note>original: *Mercurii*</note>; and with a tiny flame, you can burn a whole mountain, if it were combustible.

<margin>X</margin>
The aforementioned natural proportion must also be maintained with our <term>Mercury|In alchemy, Mercury represents the volatile, fluidic, and feminine principle of matter, not just the liquid metal</term> and <term>Sulfur|In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle</term>. Therefore the philosophers say: "Tinge so that it may tinge" <note>original: *Tinge ut tingat*</note>. This is as much as to say: you must first of all tinge your Mercury with the red tincture (which you must have prepared in the meantime, for you have plenty of time during the ongoing boiling <note>original: *decoction*</note> and <term>sublimation|The process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then condensing it back into a solid to purify it</term>, as it proceeds as a single labor). To me, this is a wonderful tincture, the likes of which you have never seen in your life, and perhaps have never even heard of: that a good and strong red tincture should cast down the mercury and yet produce a white body <note>original: *corpus*</note>. That is to say, it should allow the body of mercury to lie and remain white in the <term>crucible|A vessel used for melting substances at very high temperatures</term> after the <term>projection|The final step of the alchemical process where the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon base metal to transform it</term>.

And if one does not do this, and does not allow this white tinging to precede the rest, no man can afterwards bring this mercury to the point where it tinges anything else, neither red nor white. It is so mischievous <note>original: *schalckhafftig*</note> that it demands such a prerogative and preference: it wants to be tinged itself before all others. Furthermore, it must be tinged with the Soul of the Sun—not that gold which has been much melted, truncated, poured, and poured again

...its **body** <note>original: *corpus*</note> enters into the other, nor is it **truly** <note>original: *verè*</note> and **at the root** <note>original: *in radice*</note> united with it. <margin>X</margin>

This is what the **Author** says: both natures must rise together or at the same time under the governance of the fire.

For just as one can neither see nor hear the grass growing, even if you were to lay yourself upon the ground and keep a sharp watch by night: just as little can one perceive the **hidden motion of nature** <note>original: *Motum occultum naturæ*</note> here. Just as little can one notice the growth and increase of these two **flowers**, because of their hidden, subtle, and slow **progress** <note>original: *progreſſus*</note>. This movement cannot be **observed** <note>original: *obſervieren*</note> every hour, but only from week to week, by means of a [marker] placed there for that purpose...

# Commentaries

The second **Virtue** and **Power** is *retentive and coagulative Nature*. For Nature does not only bring to itself of its own accord that which is useful and beneficial for its continuation—provided it is not prevented by the lack of what it desires or otherwise—but it also possesses within itself the bonds with which it holds and fetters that which it attracts and brings forth. Indeed, it transforms this substance within itself (while meanwhile selecting the purest parts, separating the remainder, and leading them to the exit) and causes it to grow. And it requires here no other **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or achieve oxidation</term> or **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable or permanent under heat, preventing it from evaporating</term>. *Nature retains nature* <note>original Latin: *Natura naturam retinet*</note>, and such skill is caused by and comes from dryness, where the cold **constricts** the acquired and uniform parts and impresses them into the *earth* <note>original Latin: *terræ*</note>.

The third **Power of nature**, *in the generation and augmentation of things* <note>original Latin: *in rebus generandis & augmentandis*</note>, is the *Digestive Virtue, which occurs through putrefaction, or in putrefaction* <term>putrefaction: in alchemy, a stage of decomposition or "rotting" believed to be necessary for the rebirth and refinement of matter</term>, in moderate and tempered heat and moisture. There, Nature digests, transforms, and introduces a different kind and quality: making the raw refined, the bitter sweet, the hard soft, the harsh mild, the rough smooth, and the immature and wild domestic. What was initially useless it now makes skilled and capable, promoting it toward the final intended performance and perfection of the work, and preparing the **ingredients** for the **composition**.

The fourth **Power of nature** is the **expulsive Virtue—** <note>original Latin: *Virtus expulsiva*</note>

Furthermore, **homogeneity** <term>homogeneity: a state where all parts of a substance are of the same kind, creating a perfectly uniform whole</term> consists only of the most noble, pure, and penetrable parts (which constitute the whole). Such actions and applied labor would in no way promote the work, but would rather hinder it, or entirely burn out the natural sap and bring everything to ruin.

## concerning the little Farmer.

Likewise in animal matters <note>referring to the "animal" kingdom or living beings, as opposed to minerals or plants</note>, if you wished to cast more fire upon the **natural warmth** of the stomach, as well as the whole human body, and overwhelm it with much spice (such as those which come from India), or as some are in the habit of doing—assisting it with daily pepper and strongly seasoned foods—thinking thereby to strengthen the human's natural warmth and the stomach: such a person acts, in my opinion, foolishly, and actually cools himself down by doing so. For from such external heat and strong burning, not only is the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: *humidum radicale*; in pre-modern medicine, this was the essential fluid or "oil" that sustained the body's life-force</note> in the person consumed and burnt out, so that he must die all the sooner; but it also extinguishes the internal, innate, natural warmth. This internal heat, when compared to other fire or heat, is quite weak and subtle; it is consumed just as a larger and stronger fire extinguishes a lesser one. And as long as the pepper or other too-strong and excessive spices remain within the person and his stomach, so long is he heated and warmed. However, once these have passed from him and been expelled, the stomach is not only found back in its previous state, but is also considerably weakened thereby; it is worse and colder than ever before, since a good portion of the stomach's natural heat is daily taken away and consumed by such burning remedies.

### Regarding the Little Peasant <note>A reference to the alchemical text *Der Kleine Bauer* (The Little Peasant), often attributed to Johann Grasshoff.</note>

Rather, understand this as the other operation of the exalted union of the **Philosophical Work** <note>The *Opus Magnum*, or the process of creating the Philosophers' Stone</note>, and of the composition of the **fixed stone with the volatile stone** <note>original: *lapidis fixi cum lapide volatili*; the marriage of the stable, solid matter with the elusive, gaseous spirit</note>. # Concerning the Little Peasant #
<note>The "Little Peasant" (*Der kleine Bauer*) refers to a famous alchemical treatise often attributed to Johann Grasshoff, which emphasizes simple, natural processes.</note>

<margin>+</margin>
Whoever believes they **have the cow by the horns** <note>A German idiom (Kuh um den Sonnenzeiger) suggesting someone thinks they have mastered a complex secret or "figured it out."</note> regarding the sundial often wishes to chatter much about it. It befits you to remain mute and keep silent. Leave God’s work unjudged and unblemished. > *Indeed, if the whole sea were pure mercury, it would turn into gold by the great power of so small a grain of powder, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Quin totum si mare putus mercurius esset / Grandi tantilli vi pulueris iret in aurum, &c."</note>

As his verses roughly sound regarding such a matter, though I do not have them at hand at this moment.

These are the true **philosophical mountains** <note>original: *montes philosophicæ*</note> of the **Republic**, both **Ancient**, **New**, and **Most Recent**. Here, one does not need to enrich oneself or suck others dry through all sorts of **extortions** <note>original: *exactionibus*; refers to heavy taxation or forced levies</note>, unnoticed subtle tricks (which cut into the purses of the subjects), and assessments of the
<margin>+</margin>
people. One can also help all poor, needy people, as well as anyone else, and if one wishes, can enrich whomever one chooses.

# Commentaria #

...praiseworthy and permitted: Others are dishonest, forbidden, and proceed with inequality and injustice. Of the unpraiseworthy, unjust **occupations** <term>Handthierungen; refers here to trades, businesses, or ways of making a living</term>, we will not speak here, but rather set them aside. Among the permitted, decent, and honorable occupations, however, there are again many distinctions, where one surpasses the other—namely, by which one less harm is caused to one's neighbor through the rise and increase of the other. ### About the Small Farmer ###

...has [taken]. For whatever this person possesses, brings under his control, and holds in his hands, the other must go without and remain in want, being so much the poorer for it. This is because no more fields exist or can be found within the district and boundary where the community has gathered than what is already there; rather, the fields are measured and fixed. And those who possess many estates do not wish to enter into any communal sharing with others, but instead hold fast to <term>mine and thine</term> <note>original Latin: *meum und tuum*; the legal concept of private property rights</note>. Now, the larger the portion or piece one brings to himself—like foolish boys snatching things with a hooked stick—within that certain district, the smaller the portion with which the other must be satisfied. Consequently, one man sometimes cannot obtain what is necessary for his needs, while the other has an abundance. Thus, the fault here lies not in the <term>increase of the earth</term> <note>original: *Erdwucher*; referring to the natural growth of crops</note> or in <term>agriculture</term> <note>original: *Feldbaw*</note> <term>in itself</term> <note>original Latin: *per se*</note>, but rather a burdensome <term>incidental circumstance</term> <note>original Latin: *accidens*; a philosophical term for a secondary quality or non-essential factor that affects a situation</note> creeps in through the neighbor—specifically, through the one who conducts the business and takes up the practice of <term>agriculture</term>.

In the practice of <term>mining</term> <note>original: *Bergwerck*</note>, one is exempt from these burdens and incidental <term>circumstances</term>. In mining, no one does harm to another, nor does anyone—out of greed and the desire to have much—bring too much of the landed property to himself in a way that withdraws from the other as much as his own pile grows larger. <margin>+</margin> <term>It is in the interest of the Commonwealth</term> <note>original Latin: *Interest autem Reipub.* (short for *Reipublicae*)</note> that the common state and the welfare of a land, people, city, or village be preserved among the inhabitants as much as possible and feasible. This ensures that through the beginning and increase of one person, the other is not suppressed, and the one who is currently down may have the chance to recover himself once more. <margin>+</margin> All inequality and hindrances should be removed...

Through such inequality, the body does not merely become deformed, but it leads much more to the paralysis and destruction of the limbs, and consequently to the downfall of the entire body. To this end—I have no doubt—God Himself looked in the Old Testament, in the <term>Commonwealth of Israel</term> <note>original Latin: *republica Israëlitica*</note>, when He sought to prevent such evil and guard against future inequality. He established a <term>Jubilee Year</term> <note>original German: *hall Jahr*; the biblical year of release occurring every 50 years</note>, where all estates that had been sold, or otherwise <term>alienated</term> <note>original: *abalienirte*; legally transferred to another owner</note> and lost from the hands of the original owners, would always fall back to them in the fiftieth year. Thus, the first lords would come back into <term>possession</term> <note>original: *Posseß*</note> of their old estates without any payment, and everyone involved in buying property in the meantime had to arrange their affairs accordingly. It would not be a bad thing if this praiseworthy and useful custom were still observed among us today. For God's ancient political laws, which were given to Israel, would suit our modern politics well, as they did not flow from a lack of reason. 

But our Christians say, "Away with that! Should I always have to <term>restore</term> <note>original: *restituiren*</note> to everyone what is theirs every fifty years?" However, true Christians maintain a sense of community and do not wait to be told to observe the fiftieth or the **Jubilee Year** (for among them, every year is a Jubilee Year).

They sink shafts behind and in front, driving upwards, and occupy the <margin>#</margin> workspaces with laborers: and thus they hollow out an entire mountain range. For it commonly happens that the deeper the mine becomes, the richer the **ore** reveals itself to be, though it also demands a greater cost for **extraction** <note>original: *außfürdern*; the labor and machinery required to bring ore to the surface</note>.

### Concerning the Common Peasant.

B
<meta>catchword: Sol-</meta>

Thus, as time passed, they grew increasingly fond of **private property** <term>eygenthumb: the concept of individual ownership over communal sharing</term>, making strict use of it and conducting trade each for themselves. And despite the fact that in the beginning, they exchanged equal amounts—heap for heap—they eventually outmaneuvered one another for profit. In the end, some stores became very large while others grew quite small, and thus a very great inequality arose from this. 
These people lived by the following rhyme:

> What is Mine, is Mine? What is Thine, is Thine.

Since the **exchange of goods** <note>original: *commutatio rerum*</note> and the bartering of **wares** did not please some—as they were not satisfied with daily, necessary, and sufficient support for their bodies, their children, and their kin—they instead stretched their thoughts, minds, and ambitions further. They sought how they might enrich themselves, raise their heads above their brothers, and attain a position of power. These people invented **money** <term>Gelt: a medium of exchange used to replace direct barter</term> (which had to be made from a precious material and substance not found everywhere, namely **gold** and **silver**, so that not everyone could obtain it). This was intended to be like a **hinge** <note>original: *angel*; here referring to a pivot or axis upon which business turns</note> upon which their own and all other **trades** <term>Gewerb: business dealings or commercial occupations</term> should turn and move to and fro. By this means and invention, they could trade in distant lands and throughout the wide world, making their stores even larger. They could also gain access to many other things unknown to the common man, which would be impossible for him to attain without such means, thus allowing them to fulfill their heart’s desire and purpose.

...and the aforementioned walls or masonry stand at the top and bottom at an equal distance from one another; yet in the fundamental truth of the matter, this is not actually the case. For the **plumb lines** <term>perpendicula; vertical lines established by a hanging weight</term>, when two or more of them are placed next to one another—whether they are far apart or close together—do not actually yield **parallel lines** <term>lineas parallelas; lines that stay the same distance apart forever</term>, if one is to speak of the matter sharply and with understanding according to the dictates of geometry. Instead, they create such **lines** that would eventually intersect one another if they were to continue further; and all such lines set according to the plumb rule <note>original: *Pleynrecht*</note> finally form **the most acute angles** <term>angulos acutissimos; extremely sharp or narrow angles</term>, as they all fall together toward the middle points. After an extent or course of approximately 859 German miles <note>A "German mile" varied by region but was often about 7.5 kilometers; 859 miles (approx. 6,440 km) is a remarkably accurate historical calculation of the Earth's radius, which is roughly 6,371 km.</note>, they meet in the **center of the world** <term>Centro mundi</term> and converge upon a single point. 

Draw a **circle** <term>circul</term> and, from the middle and innermost point of this circle, extend various **lines** into equal parts, as many as you wish; see then whether you find **parallels**—that is, lines running equally at one distance into **infinity** <term>infinitum</term>—or rather, inverted **pyramids** <term>Pyramides</term>. Truly, such a matter has no significance for builders and master craftsmen <note>original: *Baw vnd Werckmeistern*</note>, nor does it bring them any danger, for they could have nothing better or more certain than the **plumb line** <term>perpendiculum</term>; and in such a large circle, this **error** <term>error</term> of **oblique angles** <term>obliquorum angulorum; angles that are not perfectly square</term> amounts to nothing in their short work. The cause of this is / that should one overstep the mentioned point / it would become an infinite, impossible task / and infinite labor <note>original: *labor infinitus*</note>, that is / it will amount to nothing. Concerning this point or center of the world <note>original: *Centro mundi*</note>, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure often cited as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: *Error occurs in the art, and its correction lies in the point.* <note>original: "Error accidit in arte, & ejus emendatio est in puncto."</note> And another says: *And unless, my son, you understand the natures through theory <term>Theory; here meaning the philosophical understanding of natural principles</term>, you will never know how to correct your work through practice <term>Practice; the hands-on laboratory work of alchemy</term>: nor understand their proportions: but rather you will fall into error, deviating through the opposing point, which lies in mere chance.* <note>original: "Et nisi, fili, per theoriam naturas intelligas, nullo tempore per practicam scies opus tuum corrigere : nec eorum mensuras intelligere : sed potius in errorem cades, deuiando per punctum contrarium, qui jacet in casu fortuito."</note> And that is precisely the point / which we call the center of the world <note>original: *Centrum mundi*</note>, which is being discussed here. For the straight lines <note>original: *lineæ rectæ*</note>, which fall upon a point from different places / from afar / if they do not rest in this point / and stand still / but instead shoot straight past / they will never come together again for all eternity, but rather move further and further from the goal and from themselves. Therefore / whoever wishes to build <note>In this context, "building" refers to both the construction of the alchemical work and the "working" or "mining" of a vein of ore.</note> should strike the cord and set the lead: (such striking must, however, happen upon the vein <note>original: "Gang." When two mines come too close to one another and would hinder each other's construction, people do not fall into discord because of it. Instead, it is customary for the **shift masters** <note>original: <term>Schichtmeister</term>, the officials responsible for managing labor and daily operations</note>, in the name of the common **shareholders** <note>original: <term>Gewercken</term>, the investors who owned shares in a mine</note>, to reach an agreement and settle with one another before the **mining judge** <note>original: <term>Bergrichter</term></note>. Indeed, they often join both disputing mines into a single company, so that they apply equal costs, build more robustly, and await equal fortune or misfortune in the name of God.

Thus, the noble **miners** <note>original: <term>Bergleuth</term></note>, with their construction and underground properties, do no harm to any other person who conducts their business up here on the **surface** <note>original: <term>superficie</term></note>. And here it is not said: "What this man has too much of, the other must lack":
<margin>†</margin>
The jurisdiction is narrow; the people and brothers are many. The rich take all the goods for themselves, and the common citizen can hardly nourish himself anymore, or obtain and purchase his own property, etc. Here it is not so: here there is field enough.

For here a large, immeasurable, unworked field lies open beneath the mountain, and it is free for anyone to **prospect** <note>original: <term>zuschürpffen</term>, to search for ore by digging trial pits</note> wherever he wishes, to set **hammer and chisel** <note>original: <term>Schlegel vnd Eysen</term>, the traditional tools of the miner</note> to the rock, and to seek a vein which he believes to be the richest for several miles around. There he may drive his **adit** <note>original: <term>stollen</term>, a horizontal tunnel for drainage or access</note>. He may awaken a new mine, or—alone or with a good companion—revive an old **pit** <note>original: <term>grub</term></note> and **receive a claim** <note>original: <term>belehnen</term>, the legal process of being granted mining rights</note>, or maintain it.
