# On the Little Peasant <note>original: "vber den kleinen Bawren"; likely a reference to the alchemical treatise *Der kleine Bauer* attributed to Johann von Laatz.</note>

Whoever desires to serve the Royal / and to show goodness / is much more powerful in Gold and Silver / and similar treasures. # On the Little Peasant.

Folio 18. The practitioner <note>original: "Laborant"; refers to the person performing the physical labor of alchemy in the laboratory</note> complains to the Peasant about the small weight of the weighed and composed materials, or even of the finished first tincture:

And he thinks it would be much better if one made a whole sack of pepper full <note>a German idiom meaning a very large quantity</note> right from the start, rather than dealing with drams and half-ounces <note>original: "quintlein vnd halblothen"; traditional small units of weight used by apothecaries and alchemists</note>. That way, one would have enough to last a while, and it would involve the same labor—indeed, almost the same time and cost. For one sees that alchemists here and there use marks and pounds <note>larger units of weight</note> in their setups.

<margin>+</margin>
But it must be known that one cannot scoop it up with a large spoon right from the beginning. For to make a great deal of this good thing in the first batch, or to weigh it for the **composition** <note>original: "Composition"; the specific proportions and mixing of the alchemical ingredients</note> and then to mix it, is an almost impossible or at least a very difficult thing. There is a reason for this, which is unnecessary to discuss further here. You surely know otherwise that sometimes there is a small trial <note>original: "Prob"; a test sample or assay</note> which can never again be found in a large quantity of that same material. You may nevertheless set up many or several glasses at certain times in the beginning—not for the sake of the quantity of the tincture <note>the potent substance used to transform base metals into gold</note>, but for other reasons: so that, if you should fall asleep, you might be woken by a bang <note>referring to the danger of vessels exploding under pressure</note>; or perhaps because one vessel has boiled over and settled into the ash <note>referring to the ash bath used to provide steady, indirect heat to the glass vessels</note>; or even so that you may have your **observations** <note>original Latin: "Observationes"</note>, **reasons** <note>original Latin: "rationes"</note>, delight, and wonder.

Just like a tiny spark or a small light, when **materials** <note>original: "materialia"</note> are added to it, consumes a whole woodpile, a whole house, or a whole forest, likewise turning it into fire and laying it in ashes. Indeed, it could burn the whole world and turn it to ash, if the world were combustible.

The wild wood grouse <note>original: "vhrhan" (Auerhahn); the Western Capercaillie, known for its dramatic mating displays</note> lets very little of his **seed** <note>original: "Spermatis"</note> fall when he is in his mating display <note>original: "Falz"; the lek or courtship period of the wood grouse</note> for the hen to consume. This, our free Peasant has also well experienced and found to be true: that as often as he has cast the little seeds into the ground and allowed them their right and necessity <note>referring to proper soil, water, and timing</note>, they have turned green and sprouted, and borne hundredfold fruit.

### Regarding the Little Peasant.

Once I saw someone who wanted to raise a whole field full of apple and pear trees from the seed <note>original: "vom Kern"</note>, and then plant them here and there across the estates. He ordered his servants that when they were drying fruit for dried slices <note>original: "Hutzelnschnitz"; typically dried pear or apple pieces used for winter storage</note>, they should save all the seeds. He thus sowed a large area with such seeds, yet obtained few young trees. The cause was that the seeds had suffocated within the small apples and pears; and although they looked as if they were very fresh, their internal invisible power and essence was extinguished because they had waited too long. Therefore, whatever was opened and collected soon after the autumn harvest all sprouted and grew; but those seeds from fruit cut open and collected after Christmas remained behind <note>i.e., failed to germinate</note>.

Before this time, I saw someone who—out of curiosity, but perhaps also out of a desire for knowledge of nature's wonders and the overflowing, high power of the Divine Word: **"Increase and multiply"** <note>original Latin: "Crescite & multiplicamini"</note>—take the roe from a fish and a medium-sized herring upon a plate. Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist known as the teacher of King Khalid</note> says: *Let the Craftsman know the kindling of his fire* <note>original Latin: *Sciat Artifex sui ignis accensionem*</note>; that is one. *Let his fire be gentle* <note>original Latin: *Sit ignis ejus blandus*</note>; that is the second. *And let it endure by burning equally through its days* <note>original Latin: *Et per suos dies æqualis ardendo perduret*</note>; that is the third.

Bonellus in the **Assembly of Philosophers** <note>original: *Turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note> says: *Truly, within it is that which amends it, unless it be put to flight by excessive fire and excessive haste.* <note>original Latin: *Revera in eo est, quod ipsum emendet, nisi fugetur igne nimio ac nimia festinantia.*</note>

And most philosophers commend a sweet fire, and with one voice testify that *haste is from the Devil.* <note>original Latin: *festinantia sit à Diabolo.*</note>

But regarding what specific inconvenience, damage, and disaster results from this—when one chooses to adopt the ways and manners of the disobedient **sloppy cooks** <note>original: *Sudelköch*; a derogatory term for careless or untrained alchemists who act like messy scullions</note> and wishes to be done with it quickly: the wise Masters say that through this, the matter becomes **vitrified** <term>vitrificieret; turned into a glass-like state by intense heat, which "locks" the substance</term>, which afterwards can not be brought to **solution** <term>solution; the critical process of dissolving the solid matter back into a liquid or "mercurial" state</term> at all, or only with great difficulty.

And in the **universal way** <term>via universali; the general or "high" path of alchemical transformation</term> it is stated: if the fire be too great, the **moist spirit** <note>original: *feuchte Spiritus*; the volatile, life-giving vapor of the matter</note> flies away (or consumes itself; it is not applied correctly, as it should be, but rather thrust by force into the **body** <note>original: *corpus*</note> or **earth** <note>original: *terram*</note>. But whatever is driven in by force is not natural, nor is it as good, **fixed** <term>fix; rendered stable and resistant to heat</term>, or constant as when it proceeds slowly and with sweetness); otherwise, the vessel may break, and the **subtle spirit** departs into the air. *A temperate fire preserves the radical moisture, while excessive fire consumes it.* <note>original Latin: *Temperatus ignis humiditatem radicalem conservat, nimius consumit. Radical moisture was thought to be the essential 'oil' or life-force of a substance.*</note>

It also deprives it of the **entry** <note>original: *Ingreß*; the ability of the alchemical medicine to penetrate and permeate base metals</note> during the **projection** <term>projection; the final stage of the Great Work where the Stone is cast upon molten metal to transmute it</term>, for with such an unholy fire the
<margin>+</margin>
**Stone** <note>original: *Lapis*</note> by no means becomes **fusible** <note>original: *fusibilis*; able to melt and flow like wax</note>, which must nonetheless be aimed for in every way.

They wish to have a **feverish fire** <term>ignem febrilem; a low, steady heat comparable to a low fever</term> and that heat with which the hen fosters the eggs placed under her, or the chick. <note>original Latin: *calorem illum, quo substrata ova sua, gallina, aut pullum, fovet*</note>

> A swimming bird is cooked slowly, a scratching bird is roasted quickly. <note>original Latin: *Nans avis est lentè, verrens torrenda repentè.*</note>

[it] cannot endure severe and sudden heat right at the start; for it contains a **viscous moisture** <note>original Latin: *humidum viscosum*</note> within itself, which must be **agglutinated** <term>agglutiniert; the process of binding or sticking parts together into a whole</term>, dried out, and **fixed** <term>sigiert; from the Latin *sigillare*, meaning to seal or make permanent</term> slowly and over a long period.

Restore to them their sweat, and light the fire again, and establish rest for them; and take care that you do not drive them away by burning with excessive fire.** <note>original Latin: *Ne incendatis pulverem igne, ne opere & motu subitò privetur. ### Concerning the green base-material, from which a *Particular* <note>A "Particular" refers to an alchemical process designed to produce a specific metal like gold or silver, rather than the "Universal" medicine or Philosopher's Stone.</note> can be obtained, and how the *Universal* <note>The "Universal" refers to the ultimate goal of alchemy: the Stone or Elixir capable of perfecting all things.</note> may be prepared.

I took true lead ore <term>Bleyerz: typically galena, the natural mineral form of lead sulfide</term>, ground it, and washed away all impurities with distilled rainwater. I dried it gently again, and then poured over it a *spirit of common salt, not rectified* <note>original: *Spiritus salis communis non rectificati*; a strong acid, likely hydrochloric acid, that has not been further purified or concentrated</note> to a depth of two fingers in a large glass flask. I placed it in gentle heat, and the water turned green. This I poured off and filtered, then allowed some of the moisture to evaporate. Afterward, I placed it in a cellar and let it form into crystals <note>original: *Christallen*</note>.

I placed these crystals in a cupel <term>Treibscherben: a shallow, porous dish used in assaying or refining metals</term> under a muffle <term>Muffel: a ceramic chamber used in a furnace to protect materials from direct flame while allowing high heat</term>, allowed the moisture <note>original: *humiditet*</note> to evaporate, and stirred it constantly.

If, however, one cannot obtain the lead ore, take one part of the *crystals of Saturn* <note>original: *Christallos Saturni*; lead acetate, also known as "sugar of lead" due to its sweet taste</note> and three parts of calcined white flint stones <note>original: *Kieselstein*</note>. Put these into a strong crucible, well-sealed <note>original: *verlutirt*; airtight closure using "lute," a clay or paste sealant</note>, and place it in a wind furnace <term>Windoffen: a furnace designed with a natural or forced draft to reach high temperatures</term>. Give it a gentle fire for half an hour, then fill the furnace with coals and let it melt strongly for two or three hours. Afterward, let it cool down together, and I found a greenish-yellow *regulus* <term>Regulum: a metallic or semi-metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</term>.

One part of this, and one part of the aforementioned crystals of Saturn, I put again into a sturdy, well-prepared crucible and let it melt once more as before. When it flowed well, I filled the furnace with coals and let it stand in the heat for several hours, and afterward let it go out. There I found a

### Process for Preparing Lead Ore According to the Philosophical Method.

<margin>+</margin>Grind the ore very fine and small; pour 2 pounds of **white wine vinegar** over it. Set it to <term>digest</term> <note>original: *digerieren*; a process of gentle, continuous heating to soften or extract substances</note>. When the vinegar has become sweet <note>This "sweetness" indicates the formation of lead acetate, historically known as "Sugar of Lead."</note>, pour it off and pour more vinegar over the ore, continuing until no more sweetness is produced. Then combine the <term>extractions</term>, filter them, and let the liquid evaporate until reduced to half its volume. Afterward, place it in a cellar to <term>form crystals</term> <note>original: *zu Christallen schiessen*</note>. Wash this salt with rainwater that has been distilled until you have several pounds of it collected. This is the <term>mercury of the philosophers</term> <note>original: *mercurius philosophorum*</note>, also called the **White Woman**.

# An Address to all the Philosophers of Germany.

<margin>+</margin>
*I now turn my speech to you, Illustrious and Magnificent Men, who shine above all other mortals in the theater of this world. You are celebrated among all students of sounder philosophy and wise men for your remarkable and admirable knowledge and possession of all manner of the most excellent things which Nature has brought forth, and which the **Supreme Creator** <term>Opifex; literally the 'Craftsman' or 'Workman,' a common term for God in alchemical literature</term> has subjected to the human intellect for contemplation. This includes every kind of art and science, and especially the **Philosopher’s Stone** <term>Lapidis Philosophici</term> and its admirable virtues. I earnestly ask—whatever land nourishes you and whoever among you reads these words—that you might deign to embrace this offspring of my intellect and my considerations, and indeed myself as well, with your protection and benevolence.*

*Within the last four years, I have seen the writings of many people come before the public, and I have seen letters written to you by those who sought your friendship. Some of them have progressed to such a point of boldness that they did not shrink from demanding entry into your illustrious Order, the **Fraternity** <term>Fraternitatem; a likely reference to the Rosicrucian Brotherhood, a secret society of alchemists and doctors that caused a literary sensation in Germany starting around 1614</term>. Yet there is almost no one among them, so far as I know, who has recited his own lessons or published any specimen of his learning to show what he has taught, or what progress he has made in this arduous and admirable study of the most secret **chemical philosophy** <term>Philosophiæ chemicæ; the high art of alchemy</term>, so as to offer a taste to those hungry for a sounder philosophy.*

*Instead, most of them are occupied with vain meanderings of words throughout their entire speech, harboring nothing of hidden things within. At the end of their writing, they finally sink down into a mere noise of words, much to the reader's disgust.*

<summary>The author shifts from technical instructions to a formal rhetorical address (an "apostrophe") to the "Philosophers of Germany," likely the Rosicrucians. He criticizes the recent influx of "bold" but ignorant authors who claim alchemical knowledge without providing proof of their practical or theoretical skill.</summary>

# ->THE ELUCIDATION OF THE TESTAMENT OF RAMON LULL<-
<note>original: "ELUCIDATIO TESTAMENTI RAYMUNDI LULLII"</note>

<margin>+</margin>
Although we have composed many books concerning the various operations of our <term>philosophical art</term> <note>A traditional term for alchemy, which practitioners viewed as the highest form of natural philosophy</note>, we nevertheless prefer this, our latest little book, to all the others. It deserves to be titled by us the *Elucidation of the Testament*. For indeed, those things which we hid with such immense wordiness in our philosophical writings, the *Testament* and the *Codicil* <note>Two of the most influential works in the pseudo-Lullian alchemical corpus</note>, we now demonstrate more clearly and elucidate most briefly in this current volume, so that there may be no further need to compose other books. 

Since the composition of our previous books was nothing other than the subtlety of a sagacious mind intended to conceal our art—which was shown so copiously in our other works—it is here led out from the shadows into a pleasant light. This is something that no other philosopher has ever dared to do with such boldness. We have divided this book into six chapters, in which the entire mystery of this art is explained with the clearest of words. These chapters are:

First, concerning the matter of our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of perfecting base metals and the human body</note>.
Second, concerning the **vessel**.
Third, concerning the **furnace**.
Fourth, concerning the **fire**.
Fifth, concerning the **cooking** <note>original: "coctione"; the process of applying heat to mature the alchemical substance</note>.
Sixth, concerning the **Tincture** and **multiplication** <note>The "Tincture" is the substance that imparts its quality to others; "multiplication" is the process of increasing the quantity and power of the alchemical medicine</note>.

<summary>This page introduces a concise alchemical treatise attributed to Ramon Lull, promising to reveal secrets previously hidden in his longer, more obscure works. It outlines six fundamental chapters covering the materials, tools, and processes required to create the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

## Chapter *First, concerning the Matter of our Stone.*

First, therefore, let us proceed to demonstrate the matter of our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical "Great Work."</note>. For we have introduced foreign things into our <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterio"; refers to the technical process or the craft of alchemy</note> through their similarities, yet in truth only one single thing exists for our stone, to which we add no foreign matter nor from which do we take anything away. We have also described three Stones—namely the *mineral*, *animal*, and *vegetable*—though there is but one single stone of our art. We wish, O sons, for this composite to signify three things: namely body, soul, and spirit. It is called *mineral* because it comes from the <term>mine</term> <note>original: "min: ra:" / "minera"; the source or ore-bed of the material</note>; *animal* because it possesses a soul; and *vegetable* because it grows and multiplies. In this substance lies hidden the entire secret of our mastery, which is the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and the **water of life** <note>original: "Sol, Luna & aqua vitæ"; these represent gold, silver, and the universal solvent or mercurial spirit</note>. And the **water of life** is the soul and the life of bodies, through which our stone is quickened and sustained; therefore we call it **heaven**, and the **quintessence**, and **incombustible oil**, and by infinite other names: since it is almost as incorruptible as the heavens in the continuous circulation of its motion. Thus, through this clear revelation, free of all circuitous speech, you have the matter of our stone.

## Chapter *Second, concerning the Vessel.*

Now we have resolved to speak of our vessel: here, son, prick up your ears so that you may grasp our meaning. Although we have revealed many types of vessels written enigmatically in our volumes, our ingenuity is nevertheless occupied with no other vessel but one alone, which we demonstrate here openly—

### *Chapter third, concerning the Furnace.*

We are about to speak of our furnace, but it will be a most difficult thing to reveal the secret of our furnace, which the ancient philosophers concealed. For we have depicted various furnaces in our books, yet we use only one single furnace, which is called the **Athanor**, the interpretation of which is "immortal fire": because it provides a fire that always lasts equally at the same degree from the beginning to the end of our stone, quickening and ripening it. Son, listen to our words, and you will understand that our furnace is composed of two parts, well-sealed at the joint of its closure. Its design is as follows: Let the furnace be made large or small, according to the quantity of the matter—for a large quantity of matter requires a large furnace, and a small quantity a small one—in the manner of a distilling furnace, with its lid firmly closed, so that when the furnace and its lid are joined, it has exactly one vent <note>original: "respiraculum"; a breathing-hole or air-vent to regulate temperature</note>, so that the heat of the kindled fire can breathe; for this reason

### *Chapter fourth, concerning Fire.*

Although we have treated the threefold fire—namely, the **natural**, **con-natural**, and **against nature** <note>In alchemy, "natural fire" often refers to the internal heat of a substance, "con-natural" to heat that assists nature, and "against nature" to corrosive or external heat</note>—and other various modes of our fire in our books: nevertheless, we wish to signify one fire composed of several things. ## *Chapter five, concerning the cooking.*

There are also many ways of preparing our stone described in our *Testament* and our other volumes—namely, **dissolution**, **coagulation**, **sublimation**, **distillation**, **calcination**, **separation**, **fusion**, **waxing** <note>original: "inceratio"; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, **soaking** <note>original: "imbibitio"; the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated</note>, **fixation**, and so on—the meaning of all of which is simply **cooking** <term>decoction: the application of steady, digestive heat to a substance over time</term>. For in our cooking alone are all these methods perfected. 

The true method of this cooking of ours is that you place the matter of the composite, according to its measure, into its vessel, furnace, and fire, cooking it continually until it reaches the completion of maturity. This will be finished in ten months without any manual labor or intervention from the beginning to the end of the entire **Great Work** <note>original: "magisterii"; the "Mastery" or supreme goal of alchemical practice</note>. 

However, by listing these various methods, we wish to signify the sublimity of our art, and to ensure that the understanding of the foolish might be surrounded by a shadowy veil. We do this lest the unworthy reach the summit of the hill of our secret, but instead persist in error until the **Sun and Moon** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun and Moon typically represent Gold and Silver, or the masculine (Sulfur) and feminine (Mercury) principles</note> are reduced into one sphere, which is impossible to happen except by the command of God.

## *Chapter six, concerning the tincture and the multiplication of our Stone.*

Finally, we shall speak of the **tincture** <term>tincture: the potent, medicinal essence of the Stone capable of transforming metals</term> and **multiplication** <term>multiplication: the process of increasing the quantity and power of the Philosopher's Stone</term>, which is the end and completion of the entire Great Work. For we have shown many ways of **projection** <note>The act of casting the Stone onto base metal to achieve transmutation</note> for our tincture in our volumes, even though our tincture is not different from multiplication, and neither of these...

<meta>catchword: ...of them</meta>

<summary>This page defines the central alchemical process as a singular "cooking" (decoction) that encompasses all other chemical operations and explains that the final goals of the work are the "tincture" and "multiplication."</summary>

<keywords>decoction, Great Work, Sun and Moon, Tincture, Multiplication, alchemical preparation, ten months maturity</keywords>

--- Page 416 ---
<meta>This page concludes the discussion from page 367 regarding the maturation of the alchemical matter, specifically addressing the final stages of the Great Work and the exponential increase of the Stone's power through the process of multiplication.</meta>

<page-num>368</page-num>

...of things, without the one being able to occur without the other. For our **stone** <term>lapis noster: the Philosopher's Stone</term> does not dye <note>original: "tingit"; in alchemy, "dyeing" refers to the transformative power of the Stone to change the color and nature of base metals into gold or silver</note> unless it is first dyed itself; and when it is dyed, its quantity is multiplied. And once our stone is multiplied, whether in its **white** or **red** form, the dyeing is performed. 

O son, cast away the shadow from your mind, so that you may understand the **secret of secrets** <note>original: "arcanorum arcanum"</note>, which has been hidden within our books through diligent industry and now emerges from the depths into the light. Hear and understand: our **multiplication** <term>multiplicatio: the process of increasing the potency and quantity of the alchemical medicine after it has been created</term> is nothing other than the repetition <note>original: "reiteratio"</note> of the composition of our primordial work. 

For in the <margin>+</margin> **first repetition**, one part of our stone dyes three parts of an imperfect body <note>an "imperfect body" refers to base metals like lead, tin, or copper</note>, and it grows and is multiplied in quantity by that many parts. In the **second repetition**, one part dyes seven parts. In the **third**, one part dyes fifteen. In the **fourth**, thirty-one. In the **fifth**, sixty-three. In the **sixth**, one hundred and twenty-seven. And it always grows and is multiplied in parts in this way, proceeding even unto infinity. 

Behold, my son, thus we clarify our writings—which until now were kept secret behind parabolic sayings—even against the usual commands of the philosophers. But we wish to be excused from their rebuke, lest by divine permission we fall under their curse. We commit this saying of our little book to Almighty God, in whose power all things reside, and who bestows all knowledge and every gift upon whom He wills. He also withdraws it, hiding it within the power of His divinity so that He does not permit the foolish or the ungodly to investigate it in the least. 

Now, son of wisdom, give thanks to God, who through His divine illumination closes and opens the human intellect: may His name be blessed, forever and ever, Amen.

<summary>This page explains the "Multiplication" of the Philosopher's Stone, revealing an exponential mathematical progression where the Stone's power to transform base metals increases with each repetition of the process. It concludes with a traditional pious exhortation, attributing alchemical success to divine grace rather than mere human effort.</summary>

<keywords>multiplication, Philosopher's Stone, tincture, dyeing, imperfect bodies, divine illumination, repetition, alchemy, transmutation</keywords>

On three types of fire the **Artist** <note>original: "Artist"; the alchemist or practitioner of the great work.</note> must pay attention to, which are found during the production of the **Stone** <note>original: "Lapidis"; the Philosopher's Stone.</note>: these he must know. One fire awakens. The other fosters and maintains. The third is an **ingredient** <note>original: "Ingrediens"</note> and tinges <note>original: "tingirt"; the alchemical process of "tincturing" or transforming the quality and color of a substance, usually into gold or silver.</note>.

How Nature in all her **works** <note>original: "operibus"</note>, in the **Animal**, **Vegetable**, and **Mineral** realms / and in the **production of creatures** <note>original: "Createn productione"</note>, always maintains a most moderate / lovely warmth: how, on the other hand, strong heat destroys and strikes down all things.

How the entire firmament moves in the union of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii"</note> and **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphuris"</note>.

Concerning **Multiplication** and **Exaltation**, that is / the increase and strengthening of the **Stone** <note>original: "Lapidis"</note>, as much in its grade and excellence / as in its quantity and abundance.

What the **Philosophical Mountains of the Republic, both Ancient, and New & most Recent** <note>original: "Montes philosophicæ Reipubl. & Veteres, & novi & nuperrimi"; likely a metaphor for the great alchemical authorities and foundational texts throughout history.</note> are.

Which among all kinds of the world's trades and handiworks / that men carry out on earth / is the most honest / the most harmless to other people and the neighbor / the most useful, praiseworthy, and highest.

The construction of the **mine** <note>original: "Bergwercks"</note> is described / what a praiseworthy / stately / important / and wonderful handiwork and labor it is.

Pious, honest folk seek / because of the unceasing wickedness of this our hemisphere / to make a passage through the **center of the earth to the Antipodes** <note>original: "Centrum terræ ad Antipodes"; referring to people living on the exact opposite side of the globe.</note> by means of the noble miners, to make acquaintance with them; or even to betake themselves there with their belongings: Understanding **Philosophers**, however, desire only the **Center of the Earth** <note>original: "Centri terræ"</note>.

Why true **Philosophers** so greatly desire to seek the **center of the world** <note>original: "centrum mundi"</note> / and what they have to expect from this.

Means and proposals / in what way one may certainly and unfailingly find the **Center of the World** <note>original: "Centrum mundi"</note> / upon which the whole burden rests.

How / when one should overstep the **center of the earth** <note>original: "centrum terræ"</note> with constant sinking <note>In a mining context, "sinking" refers to digging a vertical shaft deeper into the ground.</note> and further building / and the **Antip-** <note>Catchword for the next page: "Antipodes."</note>
